title: A Crafter's own error, caught and fixed before review begins, is explicitly not a technical issue
content:
The issue-handling process at A.1.10.2.4.7.3.1 closes with a carve-out: "if a Crafter makes an error in their original development of the Spell, but discovers their own mistake and corrects it **before the Reviewers commence the review process**, this should not be treated as a technical issue per this handling process."

Without the exception, the full machinery — classification as mistake/bug/exploit, a collusion-versus-accident judgment, evidence capture, a designated handling party, public reporting, a retrospective — would attach to ordinary development iteration. Every typo caught by its author would become a documented incident.

The incentive effect is the point, and it runs the opposite way from the Prime Spell rule at A.1.10.2.3.2.2.1.4.1.1, where inadequate self-reporting is itself a punishable incident. There the risk is concealment after an event that already touched production, so disclosure is forced. Here the risk is the reverse: penalizing self-caught errors teaches Crafters to quietly fix things, or to avoid looking too hard at their own work before handoff.

The cutoff is well chosen because it is objective and observable — review commencement is a timestamped state change, not a judgment about how serious the error was. Before it, the code is the Crafter's private draft; after it, other parties have relied on it, and reliance is what converts a mistake into an incident.
description: A.1.10.2.4.7.3.1 starts the incident regime at review handoff, so self-correction during development carries no reporting, classification or retrospective burden.
